June 15, 2026 
 
The Honorable Robert Kennedy, Jr.  
Secretary Department of Health and Human Services  
200 Independence Avenue SW  
Washington, DC 20201  
 
The Honorable Dr. Mehmet Oz 
Administrator Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services  
U.S. Department of Health and Human Services  
200 Independence Avenue SW  
Washington, DC 20201 
 
Re: Interoperability Standards and Prior Authorization for Drugs (CMS-0062-P) 
 
Dear Secretary Kennedy and Administrator Oz: 
 
Thank you for the opportunity to submit comments on the proposed rule on Interoperability Standards 
and Prior Authorization for Drugs in Medicare Advantage Organizations, Medicaid Managed Care 
Plans, State Medicaid Agencies, Childrenâ€™s Health Insurance Program (CHIP) Agencies and CHIP 
Managed Care Entities, and Issuers of Qualified Health Plans on the Federally-Facilitated Exchanges 
(CMS-0062-P). The Legal Action Center is a non-profit law and policy organization that fights 
discrimination, builds health equity, and restores opportunity for people with substance use disorders 
(SUD), arrest and conviction records, and HIV/AIDS. 
 
LAC supports CMSâ€™s proposal to extend interoperability and prior authorization standards to 
prescription drugs under these plans. Medications for opioid use disorder (MOUD) are the gold standard 
of treatment for this condition, which the U.S. Department of Health & Human Services (HHS) has 
recognized as â€œessential to address the high rates of opioid use disorder and overdose mortality.â€1 
Similarly, medications for alcohol use disorder and tobacco use disorder are critical for helping 
individuals reduce their alcohol use or facilitate smoking cessation, consistent with this Administrationâ€™s 
goals to promote greater health and wellbeing.  
 
In the midst of the ongoing overdose public health emergency,2 we commend this Administration for 
highlighting that â€œthese medications should be readily available to prevent withdrawal, treat addiction, 
and support sustained recovery.â€3 We support the provisions of this proposed rule that facilitate such 
access, and we offer the following additional comments to further ensure meaningful availability. 
 
1 U.S. Department of Health & Human Services, Office of Inspector General, â€œMedicare and Medicaid Enrollees in Many 
High-Need Areas May Lack Access to Medications for Opioid Use Disorder,â€ U.S. Department of Health & Human 
Services, OEI-BL-23-00160 (Sept. 2024), https://oig.hhs.gov/documents/evaluation/9999/OEI-BL-23-00160.pdf.  
2 U.S. Department of Health & Human Services, Administration for Strategic Preparedness & Response, â€œDeclarations of a

https://www.whitehouse.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/National-Drug-Control-Strategy-2026-1.pdf.  
2 
 
A. Extending Electronic Prior Authorization Standards to Prescription Drugs & Decision 
Timeframes 
 
LAC supports the proposal to include prescription drugs in electronic prior authorization standards. We 
agree that requiring impacted payers to support electronic prior authorization will facilitate more timely 
access to the medications people need. We also support CMSâ€™s proposal to require insurers to respond to 
prior authorization requests for drugs within 24 hours, if not sooner. We further support CMSâ€™s 
proposed decision timeframes for non-drug items for qualified health plans (QHPs) on the federally-
facilitated exchanges (FFE).  
 
In addition, we offer the following specific recommendations:  
â€¢ We encourage CMS to align the timeframe for responding to prior authorization requests for 
drugs for qualified health plan (QHP) issuers on the federally-facilitated exchanges and Medicare 
Advantage (MA) organizations to those proposed for the other impacted payers, such that all 
drug prior authorization requests are subject to the 24-hour timeframe, not just expedited ones.  
â€¢ We encourage CMS to clarify that MA supplemental benefits are also subject to these prior 
authorization rules â€“ for medications as well as other services and items â€“ to ensure these 
benefits are available without unnecessary delay. 
â€¢ We further encourage CMS to apply these requirements to traditional Medicare, such that 
beneficiaries in fee-for-service Medicare who need methadone to treat their opioid use disorder, 
for example, are not subject to life threatening delays.  
â€¢ We also encourage CMS to apply these timeframes to bundled services that include drugs, such 
as the opioid treatment program (OTP) bundle in Medicare, not just standalone medications. 
o According to a recent GAO report, approximately 87% of MA enrollees are in plans that 
may have prior authorization requirements for OTP services, with higher rates among 
those enrolled in PPOs and special needs plans.4  
o Approximately 2/3 of Medicaid fee-for-service and managed care plans have prior 
authorization requirements for OTP-based MOUD.5 
â€¢ Finally, we encourage CMS to consider a planâ€™s failure to respond within the timeframe to be a 
deemed approval, such that the patient considered approved to get the requested medication.  
o At a minimum, failure to respond within the timeframe should be considered an adverse 
decision or â€œdeemed denial,â€ such that the enrollee and provider can appeal at that time. 
Establishing consistency across all payers and more accountability will make it easier for patients, 
providers, and plans to navigate prior authorization requirements, enforce their rights when prior 
authorizations are delayed or denied, and gain timely access to medications they need. 
 
Furthermore, we encourage CMS to make clear that the use of electronic prior authorization or any other 
automated tools should not replace meaningful clinical review or lead to inappropriate denials. We 
encourage CMS to monitor use of artificial intelligence by health plans in making these determinations, 
and monitor denial and overturn rates, to identify patterns that may indicate inappropriate utilization 
management practices.

Target Behavioral Health Services,â€ U.S. Government Accountability Office, GAO-25-107342 (May 2025), 
https://www.gao.gov/assets/gao-25-107342.pdf.

Nonetheless, the ongoing use of prior authorization â€“ including prior authorization for continued use of a 
medication, or concurrent authorization â€“ remains a barrier to treatment even when done electronically 
and within 24 hours. Particularly for medications for SUD, any delay in treatment can be life 
threatening. We commend CMS, under the first Trump Administration, for requiring MA and Medicare 
Part D plans to limit prior authorizations for buprenorphine to no more frequently than once per plan 
year, and to carry such authorizations into the next plan year once they have been approved.6 As a result 
of this guidance, virtually all Medicare Part D plans that covered buprenorphine removed prior 
authorization requirements for brand and generic versions of this medication.7 Most importantly, 
removing prior authorization was then associated with an increase in the medication use, as well as 
decreases in health care utilization and expenditures related to SUD-related inpatient admissions and 
emergency department visits.8 We encourage CMS to extend this cost-effective policy of limiting â€“ if 
not removing â€“ prior authorizations for MOUD to the full range of impacted payers under this proposed 
rule, recognizing the significant role it can play in curbing the overdose public health emergency and 
saving lives. 
 
B. Improving Communications for Prior Authorization 
 
LAC supports CMSâ€™s proposal to require impacted payers to include a specific reason for denial in 
response to prior authorization requests for all drugs. However, we note that even in instances where a 
similar requirement exists, plans often fail to give a reason that is specific enough for the patient or 
provider to understand the denial such that they can meaningfully take advantage of their appeal rights. 
For example, plans often simply deny treatment as â€œnot medically necessary,â€ without specifying the 
coverage criterion that was not met or what coverage criteria they are using to make the decision. 
 
Thus, we encourage CMS to provide greater detail in these regulations on what constitutes a specific 
reason for the denial, both for drug-related denials as well as for non-drug items and services. We 
believe this would be consistent with CMSâ€™s goal of providing patients and providers with the 
information they need, while imposing minimal additional burden on payers and facilitating better 
access to appeals. We recommend CMS amend the proposed regulations to read â€œand must include a 
specific reason for the denial, including any specific criterion not met and all information necessary 
to provide a full explanation of the specific reason(s) for the denial, regardless of the method used to 
communicate that information.â€ Â§Â§ 431.80(a)(1), (2); 438.210(c)(2), (3); 457.732(a)(1), (2); 
156.223(a)(1), (2). 
 
And, similar to our recommendation that failure to meet the required timeframe constitute a deemed 
approval, we also encourage CMS to consider extending â€œdeemed approvalâ€ status to denial letters that 
fail to include the appropriate level of specificity for patients and providers to meaningfully appeal or

enforce their rights. We believe this type of consumer protection is necessary to preserve appeal rights,

Denial notices should also be written in plain language and include standardized instructions for 
requesting reconsideration or filing an appeal, including applicable timelines, deadlines, and clear next 
steps. These next steps should include what information the patient or provider would need to submit in 
order to successfully appeal the specific reason for the denial as well as covered alternatives if such a 
showing cannot be made. Patients and providers should receive notice at the same time. CMS should 
also require appropriate language-access and accessibility standards so that patients and caregivers can 
understand the decision and take timely action. 
 
We note too that we support the American Medical Associationâ€™s proposal for standardized denial notice 
templates. 
 
C. Reporting Prior Authorization Metrics 
 
LAC supports CMSâ€™s proposal to include additional requirements for reporting on prior authorization 
metrics. This information will provide regulators with a helpful overview of the extent to which a health 
plan is denying prior authorization requests. In response to CMSâ€™s request for comment, we encourage 
reporting at the plan level rather than the contract level for MA organizations. Often there are 
differences in MA plan practices, particularly when the MA organization offers plans in multiple service 
areas with different levels of access to care. We believe reporting at the plan level will ensure that these 
disparities are not masked. 
 
Moreover, we are concerned that there is insufficient specificity in these reporting requirements for 
consumers to understand the impact that prior authorizations may have on them. Prior authorization 
denial rates are high, and they routinely lead to delays in receiving care (41%), exacerbation of health 
conditions (28%), and increased worry and anxiety (more than 60%).9 Consumers need more specific 
information to make informed decisions about their health care and coverage. Accordingly, CMS should 
require that reporting data be disaggregated by factors including service type, provider type, diagnosis, 
geography, income, disability, gender, race and ethnicity, and age. At a minimum, we encourage CMS 
to disaggregate the data by protected classes, such that meaningful action can be taken to address 
discrimination. We also believe disaggregating data for medications for SUD will help CMS take 
additional steps to improve access to this gold standard of care, consistent with the Administrationâ€™s 
priorities. 
 
CMS should also require reporting on measures that more directly reflect the patient experience, 
including overturn rates, the frequency of repeat prior authorization requests, expedited-review 
outcomes, authorization outcomes following plan transitions, and, where feasible, the time between 
submission of a request and receipt of the prescribed treatment. Reporting should also capture step-
therapy-related delays and outcomes. These measures would help patients, providers, advocates, and 
policymakers evaluate whether prior authorization practices are delaying or disrupting access to care.

Another significant barrier to understanding and using prior authorization reporting data is the lack of 
consistency in website location, publication format, and terminology.10 We encourage CMS to

and analyze published data. Standardization would also allow for easier comparison across health plans, 
states, insurers, and coverage programs. 
 
D. Privacy Protections 
 
We appreciate CMSâ€™s request for information on increasing health care resiliency. The health care 
systemâ€™s increasing reliance on digital infrastructure poses both security and privacy risks to patients.

or stigmatized health conditions. According to SAMHSAâ€™s annual National Survey on Drug Use and

bad things would happen if people knew they were in treatment, such as losing their job, home, or 
children (34.4%), and being worried that information would not be kept private (33%).11 These concerns 
are well-founded: there are numerous instances of discrimination and harm against people with SUD, 
including by other health care providers and facilities.12  
 
As CMS expands the scope of information available through interoperable APIs and facilitates the 
exchange of more detailed clinical documentation, we encourage the agency to further address issues of 
data minimization, confidentiality, patient transparency, and downstream uses of health information that 
may fall outside HIPAA. Prior authorization for drugs can reveal highly sensitive health conditions,

protected by Part 2,14 in which case it is possible that no federal confidentiality protections apply unless 
the API or app is a HIPAA covered entity or business associate. We encourage CMS to strengthen and

clarify requirements for APIs and third-party applications to maintain data confidentiality in compliance

LAC appreciates CMSâ€™s request for information on step therapy, which brought up important questions

180 days.17 This rate is devastatingly low: of the 12% of MA enrollees with opioid use disorder who 
received MOUD in 2019-2020, only 17% were still receiving MOUD six months later.18 Although 
Medicaid is much better, it is still woefully inadequate: of the 69.1% of Medicaid beneficiaries with 
opioid use disorder who receive MOUD, only 57.6% continued medication for six months.19  
 
We strongly urge CMS to require that when individuals switch to a new plan, the full duration of 
treatment previously authorized by the prior plan should continue to be covered, regardless of whether 
the receiving plan has different step therapy or prior authorization criteria. That is, new payers should 
honor previously approved prior authorizations and step therapy requirements for the full duration of the 
previous authorization or 180 days, whichever is greater. There is no value in requiring patients to try 
medications that have already â€œfailedâ€ under previous insurance plans, or start from scratch when they 
have found a medication that patients and their providers agree are working. We believe recognizing and 
applying the previous payerâ€™s determination reduces the burden on providers, patients, and payers, and 
will lead to the best health outcomes for individuals. 
 
We recognize that different plans and payers use different terminology to refer to step therapy, and some 
do not use any such language but embed equivalent requirements into their prior authorization or other 
coverage criteria. We encourage CMS to clarify that any policies related to step therapy apply to any 
situations where this type of practice is used, regardless of the terminology.

analysis:
## 1. COMMENTER INFORMATION

- **Author/Organization name:** Legal Action Center (LAC); signed by Deborah Steinberg, Senior Health Policy Attorney.
- **Stakeholder type:** Advocacy Group; legal and policy organization.
- **Credentials or expertise mentioned:** LAC describes itself as a nonprofit law and policy organization focused on discrimination, health equity, substance use disorders (SUD), arrest and conviction records, and HIV/AIDS.

## 2. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

LAC supports extending interoperability and prior authorization standards to prescription drugs because faster access is especially important for medications for opioid use disorder and other SUD treatments. It asks CMS to strengthen the rule through 24-hour drug PA timeframes across payers, deemed approvals for missed deadlines or inadequate denials, more specific denial notices, equity-focused reporting, privacy protections for sensitive SUD information, and continuity-of-care protections for step therapy and prior authorizations.

## 3. REGULATORY CONTEXT

- **Specific provisions addressed:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS; PA-DENIAL-REASONS; API-USAGE-METRICS; PRIVACY-SECURITY-related API issues under GENERAL; HIPAA-PA-STANDARDS; GENERAL.
- **Regulatory citations mentioned:** CMS-0062-P; 42 CFR 431.80(a)(1), (2); 42 CFR 438.210(c)(2), (3); 42 CFR 457.732(a)(1), (2); 45 CFR 156.223(a)(1), (2); 42 CFR Part 2; 42 CFR 2.11 and 2.12.
- **Standards referenced:** FHIR; NCPDP standards; APIs; Payer-to-Payer API; data segmentation concepts; electronic prior authorization standards.

## 4. DETAILED POSITIONS

**Topic 1: Prescription drug electronic prior authorization and decision timeframes**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; PA-TIMEFRAMES-DRUGS
- **Position:** Support with modifications.
- **Rationale:** LAC believes electronic PA can speed access to needed medications, but for SUD medications any delay can be clinically dangerous or life threatening.
- **Specific request:** Apply a 24-hour timeframe to all drug PA requests for QHP issuers and Medicare Advantage organizations, not just expedited requests; apply requirements to MA supplemental benefits, traditional Medicare, and bundled services that include drugs such as Medicare OTP bundles; treat missed timeframes as deemed approvals or at minimum deemed denials that trigger appeal rights.

**Topic 2: Limits on prior authorization for MOUD and SUD medications**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DRUG-PHARMACY; PA-DRUG-MEDICAL; GENERAL
- **Position:** Modify.
- **Rationale:** LAC argues that even fast electronic PA remains a barrier for medications for substance use disorder. It cites Medicare Part D buprenorphine policies where limiting prior authorization was associated with increased medication use and reduced SUD-related inpatient and emergency department utilization.
- **Specific request:** Limit or remove PA for medications for opioid use disorder across impacted payers, modeled on prior CMS policy limiting buprenorphine PA to no more than once per plan year and carrying approvals into the next plan year.

**Topic 3: Specific denial reasons and appeal protections**
- **Provision ID:** PA-DENIAL-REASONS
- **Position:** Support with modifications.
- **Rationale:** LAC supports requiring specific reasons for drug PA denials but says generic statements such as medical necessity denials do not allow patients and providers to understand or appeal the decision.
- **Specific request:** Amend the regulatory language to require denial notices to identify the criterion not met and all information needed for a full explanation; require plain language, standardized appeal instructions, simultaneous notice to patients and providers, language access, accessibility, and deemed approval for insufficiently specific denials.

**Topic 4: Prior authorization metrics and transparency**
- **Provision ID:** API-USAGE-METRICS; GENERAL
- **Position:** Support with modifications.
- **Rationale:** LAC supports expanded PA metrics but says contract-level and aggregate reporting can mask disparities and does not sufficiently inform consumers about likely access barriers.
- **Specific request:** Require MA plan-level reporting and disaggregation by service type, provider type, diagnosis, geography, income, disability, gender, race and ethnicity, age, and protected classes; include SUD medication-specific reporting, overturn rates, repeat requests, expedited outcomes, plan-transition outcomes, time from request to treatment, and step-therapy delays and outcomes; standardize report location, file type, layout, and terminology.

**Topic 5: Privacy and confidentiality in API-enabled workflows**
- **Provision ID:** HIPAA-PA-STANDARDS; API-USAGE-METRICS; GENERAL
- **Position:** Modify/Clarify.
- **Rationale:** LAC warns that richer clinical data exchange through FHIR APIs, NCPDP standards, and patient-authorized apps can expose sensitive SUD information and may fall outside HIPAA or Part 2 protections.
- **Specific request:** Strengthen confidentiality requirements for APIs and third-party apps, prohibit sale or redisclosure for secondary purposes, evaluate data segmentation standards, clarify retention limits, permitted uses, audit requirements, minimum necessary standards for Payer-to-Payer API data, limit clinical documentation requested and transmitted, and clarify third-party app governance.

**Topic 6: Continuity of care and step therapy**
- **Provision ID:** GENERAL
- **Position:** Modify.
- **Rationale:** LAC emphasizes that continuity on MOUD is a nationally recognized quality measure and that requiring patients to restart step therapy or PA after plan changes can interrupt successful treatment.
- **Specific request:** Require new payers to honor prior authorizations and step therapy determinations for the full duration of the prior authorization or 180 days, whichever is greater, and define step therapy broadly to include equivalent requirements embedded in coverage criteria.

## 5. SOLICITATION RESPONSES

- **S16:** Directly responds to what constitutes a specific denial reason. LAC recommends requiring the specific criterion not met and all information needed for a full explanation, regardless of communication method.
- **S17:** Supports standardized denial notice templates and structured, plain-language instructions that explain appeal rights, deadlines, next steps, and covered alternatives.
- **S20/S43:** Supports 24-hour drug PA response timeframes and asks CMS to apply them consistently across all impacted payers, MA, traditional Medicare, MA supplemental benefits, and bundled drug services.
- **S29/S34/S35:** Supports expanded PA metric reporting but seeks more patient-centered measures, plan-level MA reporting, standardized publication formats, and measures such as overturn rates, repeat PA requests, expedited outcomes, plan-transition outcomes, and time to treatment.
- **S30:** Responds extensively on privacy protections, urging data minimization, confidentiality, transparency, limits on downstream uses, Part 2 protections, retention limits, audit requirements, and app governance.
- **S44/S45/S46/S50:** Raises concerns that replacing existing standards infrastructure with FHIR and NCPDP standards could expand exchange of richer clinical data without adequate confidentiality safeguards.
- **S66-S82:** Responds to RFIs on resiliency and step therapy, emphasizing privacy risks in digital infrastructure and continuity-of-care rules for step therapy and prior authorizations.

## 6. RECOMMENDATIONS

1. Finalize extension of electronic prior authorization standards to prescription drugs.
2. Apply a 24-hour timeframe to all drug PA requests across QHP issuers, Medicare Advantage, traditional Medicare, and bundled services that include drugs.
3. Clarify that MA supplemental benefits are subject to PA rules for medications and other items/services.
4. Treat failure to respond within required timeframes as deemed approval, or at minimum a deemed denial with immediate appeal rights.
5. Monitor AI and automated tools used in PA determinations, including denial and overturn rates.
6. Limit or remove PA for MOUD across impacted payers and carry approvals forward when appropriate.
7. Require denial notices to specify the exact criterion not met and all information needed to understand and appeal the denial.
8. Treat insufficiently specific denial notices as deemed approvals.
9. Require plain-language, accessible, language-appropriate denial notices with standardized appeal instructions and simultaneous notice to patients and providers.
10. Require plan-level MA reporting and disaggregate PA metrics by service, provider, diagnosis, geography, income, disability, gender, race/ethnicity, age, and protected class.
11. Add metrics for SUD medications, overturns, repeat PA requests, expedited decisions, plan transitions, time to treatment, and step therapy outcomes.
12. Standardize the location, file type, layout, and terminology for payer PA reporting.
13. Strengthen data minimization, confidentiality, Part 2, app governance, retention, audit, permitted-use, and minimum necessary protections for API data.
14. Require new payers to honor prior approvals and step therapy determinations for the prior authorization duration or 180 days, whichever is greater.
15. Clarify that step therapy policies cover equivalent requirements even if payers use different terminology.

## 7. CONCERNS & OBJECTIONS

- **Primary concerns:** Treatment delays for SUD medications, inadequate denial notices, weak appeal protections, insufficient metric specificity, privacy risks from sensitive data exchange, AI-driven inappropriate denials, and treatment disruption during plan changes.
- **Potential negative impacts cited:** Life-threatening delays for MOUD, untreated withdrawal or addiction, higher overdose risk, loss of appeal rights, discrimination or stigma from disclosed SUD information, and interrupted continuity of pharmacotherapy.
- **Implementation barriers mentioned:** Payer variation, bundled service structures, vague denial language, inconsistent reporting formats, HIPAA/Part 2 gaps for downstream app use, lack of segmentation standards, and different terminology for step therapy-like requirements.

## 8. SUPPORTING EVIDENCE

- **Data or statistics cited:** Approximately 87 percent of MA enrollees are in plans that may require PA for OTP services; about two-thirds of Medicaid FFS and managed care plans have PA requirements for OTP-based MOUD; denials cause delays in care for 41 percent, exacerbated health conditions for 28 percent, and worry/anxiety for more than 60 percent; NSDUH privacy concerns include 43.2 percent worried what people would think, 34.4 percent worried bad things would happen if treatment were known, and 33 percent worried information would not be private; only 17 percent of MA enrollees with OUD receiving MOUD were still receiving it six months later, compared with 57.6 percent of Medicaid beneficiaries receiving MOUD.
